report:
**Conclusion: yes—among people at high risk from substantial current or past smoking, regular low-dose CT (LDCT) screening reduces the chance of dying from lung cancer.** This is supported by randomized trials, so it is stronger evidence than simply observing that screened people fare better.

In the U.S. NLST, participants were current or former heavy smokers aged 55–74. Random assignment to annual LDCT rather than chest x-ray produced a **20% relative reduction in lung-cancer mortality**. The absolute difference was about 0.3–0.4 percentage points over the study period—meaning benefit is real but not every screened person benefits.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873

A separate Dutch-Belgian randomized trial (NELSON), comparing several rounds of volume-based LDCT with no screening in high-risk people, also found significantly lower lung-cancer mortality after at least 10 years. Replication in a different program supports that the effect is not a one-trial finding.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793

This evidence applies to *eligible high-risk* people, not everyone who has ever smoked. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends annual LDCT for adults 50–80 with at least a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within 15 years; stopping smoking remains far more important than screening for lowering risk.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening

CT screening also has downsides: false alarms, repeat scans, occasional invasive testing, radiation exposure, anxiety, and detection/treatment of cancers that might never have caused symptoms. Thus it should be done through a structured program with expert follow-up and shared decision-making—not with ordinary diagnostic CT or chest x-rays. The NCI likewise concludes LDCT decreases lung-cancer death risk in heavy smokers, whereas chest x-ray and sputum screening do not.  
https://www.cancer.gov/types/lung/hp/lung-screening-pdq
